:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
The temperature $T(t),$ in degrees Celsius, of a fluorescent light bulb after turning off can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}T}{\mathrm{d}t} =  -0.25(T-23)
$$

where $t > 0$ is the time, measured in minutes. If the initial temperature of the bulb is $80^\circ \rm C,$ calculate the temperature of the bulb after $4$ minutes. Round your answer to the nearest integer.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We're told that the temperature of the fluorescent light bulb is modeled by the inhibited decay equation

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}T}{\mathrm{d}t} =  -0.25(T-23).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-23} & =-0.25\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-23} & =-\int 0.25\,\text{d}t \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-23| & =-0.25t+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T - 23 > 0$ for all $t > 0.$ 
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-23 & ={e}^{-0.25t+C} \\ T-23 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-0.25t} \\ T-23 & =K{e}^{-0.25t} \\ T & =23+K{e}^{-0.25t}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K=e^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature of the light bulb was $80^\circ \rm C.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=80,$ and solve for $K{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}80 & =23+K{e}^{0} \\ 80 & =23+K \\ K & =57\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our initial value problem is

$$
T(t) = 23+57e^{-0.25t}.
$$

Finally, the temperature of the bulb after $t=4$ minutes is

$$
T(4) = 23+57e^{-0.25\cdot 4}\approx 44^\circ\textrm{C},
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
A thermometer is placed into a water bath and displays a reading of ${50}^{∘}C.$ The thermometer is then transferred to a ${10}^{∘}C$ water bath, and its reading begins to decrease. After $5$ minutes, the thermometer reading is ${40}^{∘}C.$ To the nearest minute, how long does it take for the thermometer to register a reading of ${30}^{∘}C?$ 

*Hint: You may assume that the temperature reading $T(t)$ of the thermometer decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling, where $T$ is measured in degrees Celsius and $t>0$ is the time, in minutes, since the thermometer was transferred into the ${10}^{∘}C$ water bath.*
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={10}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-10).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-10} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-10} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-10| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-10>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-10 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-10 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-10 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =10+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature reading was ${50}^{∘}C.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=50,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}50 & =10+K{e}^{0} \\ 50 & =10+K \\ K & =40\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $T(t):$

$$
T(t)=10+40{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $5$ minutes, the thermometer reading is ${40}^{∘}C.$ So, applying the condition $T(5)=40,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}40 & =10+40{e}^{-5k} \\ 30 & =40{e}^{-5k} \\ \frac{3}{4} & ={e}^{-5k} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{3}{4}\right) & =-5k \\ k & =-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the thermometer reads ${30}^{∘}C.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =30 \\ 10+40{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =30 \\ 40{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =20 \\ {e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{1}{2}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the thermometer will read ${30}^{∘}C$ after

$$
{t}_{1}=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}{-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)}≈12\,\text{min},
$$

rounded to the nearest minute.

\begin{aligned}T-74 & ={e}^{-0.08t+C} \\ T-74 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-0.08t} \\ T-74 & =K{e}^{-0.08t} \\ T & =74+K{e}^{-0.08t}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature of the exhaust pipe was ${140}^{∘}F.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=140,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}140 & =74+K{e}^{0} \\ 140 & =74+K \\ K & =66\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our initial value problem is

$$
T(t)=74+66{e}^{-0.08t}.
$$

Finally, the temperature of the exhaust pipe after $t=3$ minutes is

$$
T(3)=74+66{e}^{-0.08\cdot 3}≈{126}^{∘}\text{F},
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
A pork leg is taken out of the oven with a temperature of ${150}^{∘}C,$ and placed in a room that maintains a temperature of ${24}^{∘}C$, and its temperature begins to decrease. After $15$ minutes, the  temperature of the pork leg is ${100}^{∘}C.$ To the nearest minute, how long does it take for the pork leg to have a temperature of ${60}^{∘}C?$ 

*Hint: You may assume that the temperature reading $T(t)$ of the pork leg decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling, where $T$ is measured in degrees Celsius and $t>0$ is the time, in minutes, since the pork leg was transferred into the ${24}^{∘}C$ room.*
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={24}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-24).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-24} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-24} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-24| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-24>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-24 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-24 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-24 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =24+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature of the pork leg was ${150}^{∘}C.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=150,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}150 & =24+K{e}^{0} \\ 150 & =24+K \\ K & =126\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $T(t):$

$$
T(t)=24+126{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $15$ minutes, the temperature of the pork leg is ${100}^{∘}C.$ So, applying the condition $T(15)=100,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}100 & =24+126{e}^{-15k} \\ 76 & =126{e}^{-15k} \\ \frac{38}{63} & ={e}^{-15k} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{38}{63}\right) & =-15k \\ k & =-\frac{1}{15}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{38}{63}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the pork leg has a temperature of ${60}^{∘}C.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =60 \\ 24+126{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =60 \\ 126{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =36 \\ {e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{2}{7} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{2}{7}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{2}{7}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the pork leg will have a temperature of ${60}^{∘}C$ after

$$
{t}_{1}=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{2}{7}\right)}{-\frac{1}{15}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{38}{63}\right)}≈37\,\text{min},
$$

rounded to the nearest minute.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Given that $y > 50$ and $t > 0,$ which of the following is an inhibited decay equation?

I. $\dfrac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} t} =600+12y \[5pt]$

II. $\dfrac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} t} =600-12y \[5pt]$

III. $\dfrac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} t} =600-12y^2$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
An inhibited decay equation has the form

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} t} = -k(y - a),
$$

where $k > 0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $y > a$ for all $t > 0.$

From the given options, II is the only inhibited decay equation

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} t} =600-12y.
$$

To see this, let's factor the right-hand side of the equation. This gives,

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} t} = -12(y-50).
$$

In this case, the constant of proportionality is $k=12,$ and $a=50.$ Note that for inhibited decay, we must have $y > 50$ for all $t > 0.$

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}T}{\mathrm{d}t} =  -0.25(T-23).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-23} & =-0.25\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-23} & =-\int 0.25\,\text{d}t \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-23| & =-0.25t+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T - 23 > 0$ for all $t > 0.$ 
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-23 & ={e}^{-0.25t+C} \\ T-23 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-0.25t} \\ T-23 & =K{e}^{-0.25t} \\ T & =23+K{e}^{-0.25t}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K=e^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature of the light bulb was $80^\circ \rm C.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=80,$ and solve for $K{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}80 & =23+K{e}^{0} \\ 80 & =23+K \\ K & =57\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Finally, the temperature of the bulb after $t=4$ minutes is

$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

topics.:topic/title: Inhibited Decay Models With First-Order ODEs

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
In many real situations, a quantity decreases quickly at first, but then the decrease slows down and the quantity levels off near some fixed value.

For example, consider a cup of hot coffee placed in a room. At first, the coffee cools rapidly because it is much hotter than the surrounding air. As time passes and the coffee temperature gets closer to room temperature, the cooling slows down. Eventually, the temperature levels off and approaches the room temperature rather than continuing to decrease.

This type of behavior is described by an **inhibited decay model**.

An *inhibited decay equation* models situations where the rate at which a quantity $P$ decreases depends on how far it is from a target value $a$, called the **equilibrium value**. This equilibrium value represents the level that the quantity approaches over time.

An inhibited decay equation has the form

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}t} = -r(P-a),
$$

and an inhibited decay initial value problem has the form

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}t} = -r(P-a), \qquad P(0) = P_0
$$

where $r > 0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $P > a$ for all $t > 0.$

In this model, the equilibrium value $a$ acts as a lower bound. The solution decreases over time but never drops below $a,$ instead approaching it more and more slowly. The figure below illustrates this behavior.

![](images/1b/1b68f547db4090382b3fee626d029c619448b1c9adafe8b50312d162ff85e623.png)

**Note:** Inhibited growth and inhibited decay use the same basic idea: the rate of change is proportional to the difference between $P$ and the equilibrium value $a$. The only difference is whether the solution approaches $a$ from below (growth) or from above (decay).

Inhibited decay models can be written in expanded form. To identify an expanded equation as inhibited decay, we factorise out the *negative* coefficient of $P.$ For example, the equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}P}{\textrm{d}t} = 20-5P,
$$

*is* an inhibited decay equation for $P > 4$ and $t > 0,$ since it can be expressed with $r=5$ and $a=4$ as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}P}{\textrm{d}t} = -5(P-4).
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Inhibited Decay Equations and Initial Value Problems

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Now that we’ve practiced identifying inhibited decay models, let’s look at a classic example: **Newton’s law of cooling**.

This law describes how the temperature of an object changes when it is placed in an environment with a different temperature. Formally, it states that

*The rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings.*

This leads to the differential equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}T}{\textrm{d}t} = -k(T-T_S),
$$

where $T_S$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k > 0$ is a constant of proportionality.

Let’s put this into action. Suppose a thermometer is placed in a pot of boiling water and reads $100^\circ\textrm{C}.$ The pot is then placed in a $20^\circ\textrm{C}$ room, and the thermometer's reading begins to decrease.

Given that after $7$ minutes its reading is $60^\circ\textrm{C},$ let's model the thermometer's temperature after $t$ minutes.

In this case, the temperature of the surroundings is $T_S = 20^\circ\textrm{C}.$ So, by Newton's law of cooling, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}T}{\textrm{d}t} = -k(T-20),
$$

where $T(t)$ is the temperature reading of the thermometer and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}T}{T-20} & =-k\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{\text{d}T}{T-20} & =-k\int \text{d}t \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-20| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-20 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-20 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-20 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =20+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K=e^C$ is a constant of integration.

We'll determine the value of $K$ and $k$ in the next slide.

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
From the previous slide, the temperature of the thermometer is given by

$$
T = 20 + Ke^{-kt},
$$

where $K$ and $k$ are constants to be determined.

We're told that the initial temperature of the water was $100^\circ\textrm{C}.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0) = 100{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}100 & =20+K{e}^{0} \\ 100 & =20+K \\ K & =80\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following expression for $T(t){:}$

$$
T(t) = 20 + 80e^{-kt}
$$

We can compute $k$ using the fact that $T(7)=60{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}60 & =20+80{e}^{-7k} \\ 40 & =80{e}^{-7k} \\ \frac{1}{2} & ={e}^{-7k} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) & =-7k \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & =-7k \\ k & =\frac{1}{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the temperature, in $^\circ\textrm{C},$ of the thermometer after $t$ minutes is

$$
T = 20 + 80e^{-t\ln(2)/7}.
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $y' = 5y$ that satisfies $y(0)=3.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We first find the general solution, and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =5y \\ \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =5 \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =5\int \,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =5\int \,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =5x+C\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the exponential function to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\pm {e}^{5x+C} \\  & =\pm {e}^{C}{e}^{5x} \\  & =K{e}^{5x}\,,\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\pm e^{C}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

Now we apply the condition $y(0) = 3$ to find $K\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =3 \\ K{e}^{5\cdot 0} & =3 \\ K & =3\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $y' = 5y$ that satisfies the condition $y(0)=3$ is

$$
y = 3 e^{5x}  \,.
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\cos(3y)\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} + \sin(2x) = 0$ given that  $y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 0.$ Assume that $-\dfrac{\pi}{6} < y < \dfrac{\pi}{6} .$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We first find the general solution, and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) \\ \int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3y)\,\text{d}y & =-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3y) & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+C \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3y) & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+{C}_{1}\,,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C_1=3C.$

Now let's apply the condition $y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 0$ to find $C_1\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}y\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot 0) & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})+{C}_{1} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(0) & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+{C}_{1} \\ 0 & =0+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So we get the particular solution in implicit form:

$$
\sin(3y)   =  \dfrac {3} {2} \cos(2x)
$$
